workbookPurpose: This workbook aligns to the current SITHPAT018 Produce chocolate confectionery unit structure, performance evidence, knowledge evidence and assessment conditions. It is used with the learner assessment pack and the practical observation tools, and is not a standalone competency decision document.

currentUnitFocus.intro: Under SITHPAT018 you must prepare at least 24 individual chocolates from each of three types, using a range of production processes, centres and fillings, and at least one tempering method for couverture.
bullets: At least three different processes for producing chocolates: cut or dressed, hand coated, enrobing, made with prepared hollow shells, moulded
Each of the following used at least once across the three types: caramel, croquant, flavoured fondant, ganache, jellies, liqueurs, nougat, nuts, fruits
At least one tempering method for couverture
At least one product adjusted for a documented special customer request

howToUse: Complete the knowledge questions in this workbook.
Complete the case study and the recipe cards.
Use the product evidence matrix first, to confirm the required products will be completed and every performance evidence requirement is covered.
For each recipe card, calculate adjusted quantities where needed, complete mise en place, follow the method, and record any special-request adjustments.
Practical evidence must be observed in an operational or industry-realistic simulated commercial kitchen.
Your assessor relies on the observation tool and the theory assessment, not the recipe pages alone, when making the final judgement.
theoryQuestionsIntro: These questions cover knowledge that is required by the unit but is not assessed in your knowledge test. There are only three, because everything else is already covered there. Each question is broken into numbered parts. Every part has its own box and its own writing space. Answer every part.

theoryQuestions.heading: Question 1 — Portioning, yield and cost control
theoryQuestions.whyThisQuestionIsHere: PC 3.3 — minimise waste to maximise profitability. This performance criterion has no matching Knowledge Evidence point and is not assessed in UAT 1.
theoryQuestions.tip: Tip: Use the conversion factor method: portions required divided by recipe yield.
theoryQuestions.minimumWords: Answer every part below. Your total response must be at least 150 words.

parts.task: Select one recipe card from this workbook.
parts.responsePrompt: Write your response to Part 1 here…

parts.task: State its yield and its portion size.
parts.responsePrompt: Write your response to Part 2 here…
parts.modelAnswer: The card gives a yield of 20 pieces at a portion size of 5 gms.

parts.task: Calculate the quantities needed to produce 96 pieces, showing the conversion factor and all working.
parts.responsePrompt: Write your response to Part 3 here…
parts.modelAnswer:
Conversion factor = pieces required / recipe yield = 96 / 20 = 4.8.
Blanched almonds 37.5 gms x 4.8 = 180 gms.
Sugar 69 gms x 4.8 = 331.2 gms.
Butter 7.5 gms x 4.8 = 36 gms.
Vanilla 2.5 gms x 4.8 = 12 gms.
Total croquant mass required = 96 x 5 gms = 480 gms, which the scaled batch covers.

parts.task: Explain two ways you minimise waste during production.
parts.responsePrompt: Write your response to Part 4 here…
parts.modelAnswer:
Scale accurately and weigh to the scaled figure rather than rounding up a batch.
That way no more croquant is cooked than the order needs.
Slab the croquant to the thickness the portion size requires.
Cut with a guitar or a ruled frame so every piece is 5 gms and offcuts are minimal.
Trimmings that do come off are re-warmed into the next slab rather than discarded.

parts.task: State what couverture can be recovered and returned to the tempering machine, and what cannot.
parts.responsePrompt: Write your response to Part 5 here…
parts.modelAnswer:
Recoverable: clean tempered couverture - marble scrapings, drip tray under the dipping grid, mould-face excess
Only if it has not touched a centre, a garnish or the floor and carries no crumb.
Not recoverable: couverture containing centre, filling, jelly, nut fragments, transfer sheet residue or moisture.
Not recoverable: couverture from the nut product when the machine is next used for a nut-free run.
That material is discarded.

parts.task: Explain why waste affects the profitability of the product.
parts.responsePrompt: Write your response to Part 6 here…
parts.modelAnswer:
Every gram of couverture, nut and sugar cooked then thrown away has already been paid for.
Waste is therefore a direct loss against the margin on the box.
Couverture is the most expensive ingredient in the range.
A batch over-tempered, out of temper or contaminated cannot be resold and takes the whole cost with it.
Waste also costs the labour and machine time spent producing it.
It can put the order short, so the product has to be made twice.

assessorBenchmark.title: ASSESSOR BENCHMARK — Theory Question 1
whatSatisfactoryLooksLike: All six parts answered; total at least 150 words.
A workbook recipe card named with its MVC number, yield and portion size correct.
Conversion factor = pieces required divided by recipe yield.
Every ingredient scaled by it, with the working visible.
Two genuine and different waste-minimisation methods given.
Recoverable and non-recoverable couverture distinguished, with a reason.
Waste linked to margin, to couverture as the most expensive ingredient, and to labour or rework.
minimumAcceptableResponse: A named recipe card with the correct yield and portion size.
Correct conversion factor, at least three ingredients scaled, working shown.
One correct example each of recoverable and non-recoverable couverture.
One sound reason waste affects profitability.
criticalErrors: Yield or portion size does not match the named recipe card.
Conversion factor inverted (yield divided by pieces).
Scaling applied to some ingredients but not others, without explanation.
Couverture that touched a centre, garnish or nut product called recoverable.
Profitability answered as waste is bad, with no cost reasoning.
Total response under the 150 word minimum.
assessorBenchmark.workedAnswerKeyAndTolerance:
Worked key - Question 1, Part 3 (model uses Recipe 12, Almond croquant MVC1856, yield 20).
Conversion factor = 96 / 20 = 4.8.
Blanched almonds 37.5 x 4.8 = 180 gms.
Sugar 69 x 4.8 = 331.2 gms.
Butter 7.5 x 4.8 = 36 gms.
Vanilla 2.5 x 4.8 = 12 gms.
Cross-check: 96 pieces x 5 gms portion = 480 gms of croquant required.
Tolerance: quantities correct to one decimal place.
Conversion factor may be expressed as 4.8 or 24/5.
Different card selected: recalculate against that card's yield - the method, not the figures, is judged.
Card with no stated yield (Recipes 1 to 3): redirect the learner to a card that has one.
assessorBenchmark.exampleCommentSatisfactory: Selected MVC1856, quoted yield and portion size correctly, applied a conversion factor of 4.8 with working shown, gave two distinct waste controls, separated clean recoverable couverture from material carrying centre or nut fragments, and reasoned profitability from ingredient cost and rework - S.
assessorBenchmark.exampleCommentNotSatisfactory: Conversion factor calculated as 20 divided by 96, so the scaled quantities were wrong, and recovered couverture from a dipped product called always returnable. Re-attempt Parts 3 and 5: divide pieces by yield, and state what disqualifies couverture from return - NS.

theoryQuestions.heading: Question 2 — Special customer request adjustment
theoryQuestions.whyThisQuestionIsHere: Special-request coverage required by this workbook. Not assessed in UAT 1.
theoryQuestions.tip: Tip: The six scenarios are in the Special customer request table earlier in this workbook.
theoryQuestions.minimumWords: Answer every part below. Your total response must be at least 150 words.

parts.task: Select one scenario from the special customer request table.
parts.responsePrompt: Write your response to Part 1 here…

parts.task: Select one recipe card the scenario can be applied to.
parts.responsePrompt: Write your response to Part 2 here…

parts.task: Explain the request and what the customer needs.
parts.responsePrompt: Write your response to Part 3 here…
parts.modelAnswer:
Six guests at the Friday function have a severe tree nut allergy.
They need a portion of the order containing no tree nuts at all.
It must not have been exposed to tree nuts during production, storage or packing.
A severe allergy is not a preference — trace contact can cause anaphylaxis.
The requirement is complete exclusion and complete separation.
It must be documented so front of house can identify the pieces and answer for them.

parts.task: Explain the adjustment you make to the recipe.
parts.responsePrompt: Write your response to Part 4 here…
parts.modelAnswer:
Keep the croquant method; replace blanched almonds one for one by weight with toasted pepitas (pumpkin seed).
Pepitas caramelise and set in the same way.
For 12 nut-free pieces the conversion factor is 12 / 20 = 0.6.
Pepitas 22.5 gms, sugar 41.4 gms, butter 4.5 gms, vanilla 1.5 gms.
Coat in dark couverture from a freshly opened bag tempered in a cleaned machine.
Not from the couverture used for the nut products.
Record the substitution and the reason on the recipe card.

parts.task: State the food safety and allergen controls you put in place.
parts.responsePrompt: Write your response to Part 5 here…
parts.modelAnswer:
The nut-free batch is made first, at the start of the shift.
Bench cleaned and sanitised beforehand; dedicated utensils, separate chopping board, colour-coded tongs.
Couverture tempered from a new sealed bag in a machine stripped, washed, sanitised and dried.
No recovered couverture is used.
Containers labelled NUT FREE with date and batch, sealed, shelved above the nut products
Pieces boxed separately and labelled; the substitution recorded so the allergen declaration is accurate.

parts.task: Explain how you keep the product quality and appearance acceptable after the change.
parts.responsePrompt: Write your response to Part 6 here…
parts.modelAnswer:
Pepitas are close to almonds in size, oil content and behaviour in a caramel.
The croquant sets to the same brittle texture and cuts to the same 5 gms portion, method unchanged.
Toasted to the same colour, so the flavour is comparably nutty rather than raw.
Cut pieces are the same dimensions as the almond version.
Hand dipped in the same dark couverture and dusted the same way.
Finished piece matches the box for size, gloss and finish - the guest is not visibly singled out

assessorBenchmark.title: ASSESSOR BENCHMARK — Theory Question 2
whatSatisfactoryLooksLike: All six parts answered; total at least 150 words.
One of the six scenarios in the special customer request table named.
A recipe card the scenario genuinely applies to, named with its MVC number.
Request explained as what the customer needs, not just what is removed.
Adjustment specific, with substitute ingredients and quantities.
Controls cover production order, separation, dedicated equipment, labelling and storage.
Quality answer shows the product still matches the range in texture, size and appearance.
minimumAcceptableResponse: A named scenario and a compatible named recipe.
A clear statement of the customer need.
At least two allergen or food safety controls.
One credible point about maintaining quality.
criticalErrors: Scenario paired with a recipe it cannot apply to.
For example, a gluten-free request against a recipe with no flour component.
Allergen answer relies on cleaning alone, with no separation or sequencing.
A severe allergy treated as a preference.
A substitution given with no quantity.
Adjusted product called acceptable when it fails the portion or presentation standard.
Total response under the 150 word minimum.
assessorBenchmark.exampleCommentSatisfactory: Selected the nut allergy scenario against MVC1856 with a pepita substitution and quantities, then covered production first on a cleaned bench, dedicated utensils, couverture from a new bag, labelling and separate storage. Explained why the substitute holds texture and portion size - S.
assessorBenchmark.exampleCommentNotSatisfactory: Controls relied on washing the bench afterwards, the nut-free batch was made after the almond croquant, and no substitute quantity was given. Re-attempt Parts 4 and 5: give the substitute with its scaled quantity and place the batch in the running order - NS.

theoryQuestions.heading: Question 3 — Allergen cross-contact control between products
theoryQuestions.whyThisQuestionIsHere: Allergen cross-contact is not a Knowledge Evidence point of SITHPAT018 and is not assessed in UAT 1, but it applies directly to a shift producing nut and nut-free products together.
theoryQuestions.scenario: Your shift produces almond croquant, raspberry jelly squares and caramel bonbons using the same bench, the same tempering machine and the same enrober.
theoryQuestions.tip: Tip: Recovered couverture cannot go back into a product whose allergen declaration does not list nuts.
theoryQuestions.minimumWords: Answer every part below. Your total response must be at least 150 words.

parts.task: Explain how you sequence the three products to control allergen cross-contact.
parts.responsePrompt: Write your response to Part 1 here…
parts.modelAnswer:
Nut-free work first, then the products containing no nuts, then the nut product last.
On this shift: raspberry jelly squares, then caramel bonbons, then almond croquant.
Nothing that follows the nut product can then pick up its residue.
Once the croquant is made, no further product starts on that bench or machine until a full clean-down.
The controls are built into the running order rather than relying on cleaning alone.

parts.task: Explain how you separate the nut components on the bench.
parts.responsePrompt: Write your response to Part 2 here…
parts.modelAnswer:
Almonds weighed and toasted on a dedicated bench at the far end of the section.
Away from the moulding and enrobing line.
Their own board, tray, knife and tongs, kept in a labelled container.
Kept sealed and labelled until the moment of use; never carried open across the section.
Anyone handling them changes gloves and apron before returning to other work.
Nut waste goes straight into a lidded bin rather than sitting on the bench.

parts.task: State what cleaning is done between products, and when.
parts.responsePrompt: Write your response to Part 3 here…
parts.modelAnswer:
Between products: bench, boards, utensils, scales washed hot, rinsed, sanitised, dried; cloths changed
After the nut product: a full clean-down of the bench, the dipping forks and the marble.
The tempering machine bowl and auger stripped, washed, sanitised and dried before any other couverture goes in.
The enrober belt and pan washed and sanitised at the end of the run.
Cleaning is done immediately after each product, not left until the end of the shift.

parts.task: Explain what happens to couverture recovered from the nut product.
parts.responsePrompt: Write your response to Part 4 here…
parts.modelAnswer:
Couverture recovered from the almond croquant carries nut protein, however clean it looks.
Dipped pieces shed fragments into the bowl and the drip tray.
It is kept as nut-containing couverture, labelled CONTAINS TREE NUTS with the date.
Returned to the tempering machine only if the next product in that machine also declares tree nuts.
Never into the nut-free batch or a product whose allergen declaration does not list nuts.
If no nut-declaring product is left to run, it is discarded.

assessorBenchmark.title: ASSESSOR BENCHMARK — Theory Question 3
whatSatisfactoryLooksLike: All four parts answered; total at least 150 words.
Nut-free and non-nut products sequenced before the nut product.
Explains why the running order is itself a control.
Separation covers dedicated area, dedicated equipment, sealed labelled storage, glove or apron changes.
Cleaning states what, with what, and when - immediately between products.
Full clean-down after the nut product, including tempering machine bowl and auger.
Recovered nut couverture carries nut protein; nut-declaring products only, or discarded.
minimumAcceptableResponse: Running order places the nut product last, with a reason.
Cleaning stated as between products, not at the end of the shift.
Recovered nut couverture cannot enter a nut-free product.
criticalErrors: Nut product sequenced before nut-free work.
Cleaning described only as at the end of the shift.
Recovered nut couverture called usable once strained or remelted.
Cross-contact treated as hygiene rather than allergen control.
Total response under the 150 word minimum.
assessorBenchmark.exampleCommentSatisfactory: Sequenced jelly, then caramel, then croquant with the reason stated, described a dedicated nut bench with its own equipment and sealed labelled storage, set out cleaning between products including a full strip of the tempering machine, and restricted recovered nut couverture - S.
assessorBenchmark.exampleCommentNotSatisfactory: The croquant was produced first and the controls relied on cleaning afterwards, and recovered couverture was called safe to reuse once remelted. Re-attempt Parts 1 and 4: place the nut product last with a reason, and state what happens to nut-bearing couverture - NS.

specialRequestTable.heading: Special customer request scenarios
specialRequestTable.intro: At least one recipe in this workbook must be produced with a documented special customer request adjustment. Record the request, the requirement identified, the change made, and how product quality and food safety were maintained.
rows: Remove tree nuts and nutbased garnishes; substitute with seeds or safe inclusions; prevent cross-contact.
Modify garnish, piping or finish for a safer texture while keeping flavour and presentation appropriate.
Remove non-compliant items such as alcohol or gelatine and use compliant alternatives.
Reduce portion size or use a lighter finish where quality remains acceptable.
Use a compliant flour blend and prevent gluten contamination.
Replace dairy, gelatine or egg components where the product can be adjusted appropriately.
Ingredient replacements and expected product change.

observationInstrumentCover.heading: Assessment instrument — observation of practical competency

rows: Golden Wattle Group Pty Ltd trading as Meridian Vocational College, RTO 45039, CRICOS 03551M
SITXFSA005 Use hygienic practices for food safety
MVC training facility — simulated commercial kitchen

whatThisInstrumentIs: This instrument records what the assessor sees you do in the kitchen.
There are eight observation sheets, one for each element of the unit.
Each sheet lists the actions the assessor must see, and each action is marked separately.
Practical competency cannot be judged from written work alone.
This instrument is used together with your Recipe Workbook, the knowledge assessment, and the Student Assessment Record.
All of them must be satisfactory before a result of competent is recorded.
instructionsForAssessor: Confirm the assessment date with the student at least two working days beforehand.
Give the student the recipes at least one week before the assessment.
Explain the scenario and any special requests that apply to the recipes.
Observe the student across the whole task. Do not mark from memory afterwards.
Mark each action S (satisfactory) or NS (not satisfactory) as you observe it.
Write a note against any action marked NS, so the student knows what to repeat.
Ask questions during the task where you need to confirm understanding, and record the answer in the notes column.
Apply the Principles of Assessment and the Rules of Evidence throughout.
Record any reasonable adjustment in the space provided on each sheet.
instructionsForStudent: Read the recipes and this instrument before the assessment day.
Ask your assessor about a reasonable adjustment before the assessment begins.
Work at your normal pace. The assessor will watch and take notes.
You may be asked questions while you work. Answer in your own words.
If an action is marked not satisfactory, your assessor will tell you what to repeat and when.
howMarked: S — satisfactory. The assessor saw the action performed to the required standard.
NS — not satisfactory. The action was not performed, or not to the required standard. A note must be written explaining what was missing.
Every action must be marked S before the sheet is judged satisfactory.

observableIndicators.exampleCommentSatisfactory: Stated 31 degrees C for milk couverture, reserved the seed from the total, melted to 40 degrees C and stirred it in fully. Read a test strip before committing the batch, then re-checked three times and held the band. All actions S.

extractionNotes: Principles table: the heading reads 'Principles of assessment & rules of evidence' but the table carries FOUR rows and FOUR concepts only — Fairness, Flexibility, Validity, Reliability. There are no rules-of-evidence rows (no Valid, Sufficient, Authentic, Current). Nothing was added; the source has four rows, two columns.

Assessment conditions: the source reads 'industryrealistic' as one word (a line-break artefact in the underlying document). Reproduced verbatim. The same phrase appears hyphenated as 'industry-realistic' in 'How to use this workbook'.
Theory questions: there are exactly three. Question 2 IS the 'Special customer request adjustment' question required by the brief; all six of its Parts are captured.

Question 2's Tip says the six scenarios are 'earlier in this workbook', but in the source document order the Special customer request scenarios table actually appears AFTER the theory questions (after the case study and the product evidence matrix). Reproduced verbatim without correction.
Each theory Part in the learner workbook carries its own writing space labelled 'Write your response to Part N here…' — captured as 'responsePrompt'. The em-ellipsis character is preserved.

Model answers in the assessor guide are each prefixed with the label 'MODEL ANSWER — '. That label has been stripped and only the answer text stored in 'modelAnswer'; the label is a rendering artefact, not answer content.

The assessor guide's theory benchmarks are per-QUESTION, not per-Part. They are stored on each question as 'assessorBenchmark' with the guide's own sub-headings. Only Question 1 carries a 'Worked answer key and tolerance' panel; Questions 2 and 3 have none, so that field is null for them.
Special customer request table: six scenarios, four columns. Scenario 1 reads 'nutbased garnishes' as one word in the source; reproduced verbatim.
Product evidence matrix: eight columns, ten rows. EVERY cell is pre-filled in the source — no cell is left blank for the learner to complete. The intro paragraph is a single sentence.

Observation instrument cover: the detail table has only FOUR rows — RTO, Unit assessed, Pre-requisite unit, Location of assessment. There is NO qualification row, NO student name/ID row and NO assessor name row on this cover in the source. None were invented.

Observation instrument cover: 'What this instrument is' appears as continuous prose in the text dump, so individual bullet/paragraph boundaries are not recoverable. It has been split at sentence boundaries; the wording is verbatim but the item breaks are inferred.

Observation headings in the LEARNER workbook use the form 'Observation N' + TAB + element title (confirmed at byte level). The ASSESSOR guide uses 'Observation N — element title' with an em dash. The learner form is stored in 'headingForm'; 'elementTitle' holds the title alone.

Observation closing blocks: each sheet in the learner workbook closes with 'Result for this observation' and the row 'Result ☐ Satisfactory        ☐ Not satisfactory'. There is NO trainer signature row and NO date row on any of the eight sheets in the source, so 'trainerSignatureAndDateRow' is null throughout. (Note: MVC_HOUSE_STANDARD.md section 8 expects 'result and trainer signature rows' — the source workbook does not have the signature/date row. Flagged, not fabricated.)
'Assessor notes' is a COLUMN on every criteria row, not a separate closing block; there is no free-text assessor notes box at the foot of the sheets.

Assessor indicators are per-SHEET in the assessor guide ('OBSERVABLE INDICATORS — Observation N'), not per criteria row. Every row-level 'assessorIndicator' is therefore null, and the sheet-level panel is stored on each observation as 'observableIndicators' with its four labelled fields. No row-level indicator was invented.

Row counts per observation sheet, as they appear in the source: Obs 1 = 11, Obs 2 = 13, Obs 3 = 11, Obs 4 = 11, Obs 5 = 8, Obs 6 = 7, Obs 7 = 4, Obs 8 = 9. Total 74 criteria rows. The text dump repeats the header line 'PC The student did this S NS Assessor notes' mid-table on Obs 2, 3 and 4 where the table breaks across a page; those repeats are header rows, not criteria rows, and are not counted.

Observation 4's indicator panel in the assessor guide spells temperatures as 'degrees C' rather than using the '°C' symbol; the observation criteria rows themselves use '°C'. Both reproduced exactly as found.

Out of scope for this extraction and therefore not captured here: the assessment cover sheet, the title page, the Case Study Assessment section (overview, scenario at a glance, the situation, what you must do, and the three Recipe Requirements / Ingredients and Quantity Adjustments template sets), the fifteen recipe cards, and the assessor-guide-only sections (assessor judgement guidance, sample-marked Observation 4 sheet, oral questioning record, UARS result sheet, principles/rules/assessor requirements, assessor declaration and build notes).
'La Meridienne Patisserie, Rundle Street, Adelaide' appears only in the Case Study section, which is outside this extraction's scope; it does not occur in any section captured here.

assessorRecords.intro: These three records are completed by the assessor, not the student. They exist because the observation sheets are organised by element while the Performance Evidence is organised by requirement - one sheet per element cannot show which dish demonstrated which requirement, on what date, or how many portions were produced within the time constraint. The product evidence matrix does not close that gap: the student completes it, and it states what the dishes could demonstrate, not what the student did.
